## Structure and components

- [statement] Foltynie and colleagues describe MDS UPDRS Part 1 as capturing non-motor symptoms, Part 2 as capturing motor impact on daily living, Part 3 as clinician-assessed motor severity, and Part 4 as motor complications. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-02-08) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13438061/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease research ecosystem and health systems: clinical trial design and endpoints, regulatory pathways at FDA and EMA, patient registries and research participation, global burden, cost and access to care
- [statement] The EJS ACT-PD registry specifies the equally weighted combined MDS-UPDRS Parts I and II as its primary outcome measuring progression between active-treatment and placebo arms. ## How it works

- [statement] The EMA guideline states that dopamine uptake or receptor-density imaging is insufficient as a surrogate because correlation with meaningful persistent clinical change has not been established. ## Problems, failure modes and limitations

## Research summary — Clinical trial design: endpoints, enrichment and platform trials in PD

Parkinson’s trial design separates symptomatic improvement from sustained changes in disease progression. Clinical scales, patient-relevant milestones and carefully defined enrichment strategies serve different purposes. The cited studies illustrate why wash-out and delayed-start findings need cautious interpretation, why clinically important change thresholds depend on the instrument and study method, and why imaging enrichment does not establish a surrogate endpoint. The platform trial combines interim treatment decisions with a registered combined rating-scale primary outcome.

## Research summary — Global burden, economic cost and access to PD care

This concept connects estimates of the global Parkinson disease burden with economic costs and access to treatment. WHO and Global Burden of Disease analyses describe substantial populations living with the condition; the BMJ study models future prevalence. The economic studies quantify societal costs in the United States, with the later report covering both Parkinson disease and atypical parkinsonism. WHO describes barriers to medicine access, while studies of African essential medicines lists, Nigerian pharmacies and Middle Eastern physicians examine different aspects of access. Listing a medicine does not guarantee access, and physician perceptions do not substitute for objectively verified availability. Estimates remain attributed to their own studies, populations and methods.

## Research summary — Patient registries and research participation: PPMI and trial finders

Parkinson’s research participation spans observational biomarker cohorts, online studies, trial matching tools and genetic research. PPMI combines longitudinal biomarker research with online, mailed-screening and in-person participation routes. Fox Trial Finder connects volunteers with recruiting studies, while Fox Insight collects self-reported health experiences online. PDBP and the AMP Parkinson’s Disease platform support sharing of research data, and PD GENEration offers genetic testing and counseling. Participation opportunities coexist with incomplete demographic reporting and practical barriers documented in specific research populations. Foundation listings do not constitute endorsement of participation.

## Research summary — Regulatory pathways (FDA, EMA) for PD therapies

Regulatory evidence for Parkinson’s therapies spans medicinal-product guidance, biomarker support and qualification, drug applications and approvals, and device supplements. EMA distinguishes its effective guideline from a concept paper proposing revision. Biomarker support letters have a narrower meaning than qualification. Concrete examples illustrate FDA drug applications, a device supplement, and distinct European authorisation routes. Sponsor announcements are attributed separately from regulator records. FDA’s discussion of real-world evidence also documents limits on its use in labeling.
